mapsSub: Maps appear less often than charts in Task 1, but examiners expect the same precision: compass points, the right verb for position, and paraphrases that don't cross a line the language won't allow.
mapsIntroTitle: Reading the map before you write
mapsIntroSub: Four rules from the lesson that examiners check closely.
m1P: It's passive voice, present tense. Vary it with "is situated" or "lies" — never change it to "locates".
m2H: A town is never a city
m2P: "Town centre" can only become "the centre of the town" — "city centre" is factually wrong if the map says town.
m3P: If the key says "road", write "road" — not "street" or "lane". Each names a different kind of route, and the examiner checks your words against the map.
m4H: Capitals in the key, lower case in your writing
m4P: Keys often label features in capitals. Write them as ordinary prose: HOUSING AREA becomes housing area — but DARTFORD becomes Dartford, because a name keeps its capital.
dataSub: When a chart doesn't give you a clean number, an examiner still expects precision — not a made-up figure. This module drills the five-band vocabulary of approximation.
dataIntroSub: Anchor every expression to how far the value sits from the reference number.
d1P: A value a long way below the marker.
d2P: A value only a little below the marker.
d3P: Use this band only when you genuinely can't tell if it's above or below.
d4P: Mirror the "under" bands on the other side of the marker.
dataChartNote: The chart these questions describe — read the bars against the gridlines.

m_mcq0: "Is located" is passive voice in the present tense. Many students mistake it for a past-tense form and wrongly change it to "locates" — that's a basic grammar error IELTS penalises.
m_mcq1: Keep the word town: "the centre of the town" works, "city centre" is factually wrong, and the outskirts are the opposite of the centre.
m_mcq2: "Street" names a different kind of road, usually a built-up one inside a town. Keep the key's own word, so the examiner can match your sentence to the map.
m_mcq3: Capitals in the key are just a labelling style. Reproducing them as capitals in flowing prose would be grammatically incorrect — they need to be written in normal lower case, unless the word is a name, like Dartford.
m_mcq4: "Dartford" and "population" are both singular: Dartford HAS 60,000 inhabitants, and its population IS 60,000. The other options mismatch subject and verb.
m_cloze0: Position takes the passive: B IS SITUATED. "Locating" and "locates" are active forms, and "situation" is a noun — "locates" is the error the lesson warns against.
m_cloze1: "Runs through" is the natural collocation for a railway or road crossing a town from one side to the other.
m_cloze2: On the map the railway crosses the town centre, so it runs through it. "Along" would mean beside it, and "under" would mean in a tunnel.
m_cloze3: "Living" correctly forms the present participle after "people", describing who currently resides there.
m_cloze4: The lesson's model sentence places B just outside the housing area, meaning beyond its edge — not within it.
m_reorder0: Position, then compass direction, then the reference point, then the extra detail — the standard order for a location sentence.
m_reorder1: Subject, collocation verb, place, then the direction of travel.
m_reorder2: A relative clause ("which has...") adds detail about the town centre after stating A's position.
m_reorder3: Subject plus singular verb "has", then the population figure, then its source.
m_reorder4: A variation using "is situated" instead of "is located", keeping the same clause order.
d_mcq0: Examiners check accuracy. If the chart doesn't clearly show 28%, writing that exact figure is a fabricated statistic — use approximation language instead.
d_mcq1: "Well under" and "considerably less than" signal a large gap below the marker, unlike the milder "just under" band.
d_mcq2: This band exists specifically for uncertainty about direction — not knowing whether a value sits above or below a given point.
d_mcq3: "Just over" and "marginally above" describe a small gap above the marker, mirroring "just under" on the other side.
d_mcq4: Using varied, precise expressions for over/under/about demonstrates a wider vocabulary range, which is directly rewarded in the marking criteria.
d_cloze0: The men's bar sits close to but below 30%, so the mild "just under" band fits — not the much larger gap of "well under".
d_cloze1: When you can't tell whether a value sits above or below the marker, "about" is the correct, honest choice.
d_cloze2: The men's figure sits a little above 20%, matching the "just over" / "slightly over" band rather than a large gap.
d_cloze3: Men over 40 sit well above 40% against just under 30% for the youngest men, and women show the same gap: "considerably higher than" is the size of it.
d_cloze4: The lesson stresses that inaccurate or invented data directly lowers your Task Achievement score.
d_reorder0: Subject, verb, the data being shown, how it is divided, then the date — a standard opening description.
d_reorder1: Time/category first, then the approximated figure, then who the figure refers to, then the verb.
d_reorder2: Category, verb, approximated figure, then an honest note about the uncertainty — exactly the caution the lesson recommends.
d_reorder3: Subject, verb phrase, the approximated figure, then a comparison back to the previous data point.
d_reorder4: A cause-and-effect warning sentence: the inaccurate subject, where it appears, then the consequence.
